\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Five confidence signals achieve reliable NER quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC above 0.81), but selection gains are associated with low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment (approximate thresholds: ${<}$15\% and $\rho \gtrsim 0.3$); LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD where both hold.
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists but the gap persists; content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} may be needed to close it.
As models improve, degeneracy rises and the selection window narrows.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP tends to achieve gains when both factors are present (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 59.1\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 59--89\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation provides the primary evidence that both factors appear independently associated with selection success: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 12.5\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Approximate boundaries from our data: degeneracy ${<}$15\% and $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$; temperature and training convergence are controllable levers (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 59.1\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to selection.}
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS) that gates on within-instance LP range yields modest gains but cannot overcome weak alignment (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
Entity-level majority voting, where the merged output includes all entities present in ${>}N/2$ samples, yields $+0.76$~pp on SciERC (5.8\% gap recovery) but $-0.64$~pp on CoNLL and $-3.21$~pp on Few-NERD. On degenerate subsets, merge is uniformly negative across all three datasets; entity-level aggregation cannot bypass the diversity bottleneck.
Hidden state probes (\S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}) confirm richer information exists ($+37$\% correlation) yet the gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ LP's $+4.8$\%), reinforcing the capability-diversity tension.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, kim2026reasc, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} all rely on answer-level agreement; \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt to difficulty-aware settings; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on fusion rather than selection.
We extend self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identify the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, where degeneracy is most pronounced and is modulated by task structure and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency for QA/summarization; our supervised signal combination baseline (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) suggests combination strategy is not the bottleneck.
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden, yun2025price}.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC above 0.81 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} learn per-sample scoring; reward model ensembles mitigate but do not eliminate reward hacking \cite{eisenstein2023helping}. Our LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7.2\%, selection still shows no improvement at $\rho{\approx}0.24$) suggests that, within the five unsupervised signals studied, increasing output diversity alone is insufficient.
Fine-tuning contributes to degeneracy, analogous to diversity collapse in RLHF \cite{kirk2024understanding}; constrained structured outputs limit the diversity that temperature scaling \cite{holtzman2020curious} or diverse decoding \cite{vijayakumar2018diverse} can recover.

Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension} but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
We cover 4B\textendash 8B scale; whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closed-source APIs is untested. Larger models may produce more diverse samples (potentially reducing degeneracy), but their LP-quality alignment behavior is unknown, and these two factors may shift in opposite directions.
Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}), confirming the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.
Our selection experiments use 3 training seeds for Few-NERD and CoNLL (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.04$~pp for LP selection), confirming robustness on the key positive and negative datasets; SciERC uses 1 primary seed with high seed sensitivity ($\sigma{=}0.48$~pp, $n{=}529$), reflecting limited within-seed statistical power.
Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP tends to achieve gains when both factors are present (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 59.1\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 59--89\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation provides the primary evidence that both factors appear independently associated with selection success: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 12.5\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Approximate boundaries from our data: degeneracy ${<}$15\% and $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$; temperature and training convergence are controllable levers (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 59.1\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to selection.}
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS) that gates on within-instance LP range yields modest gains but cannot overcome weak alignment (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
Entity-level majority voting, where the merged output includes all entities present in ${>}N/2$ samples, yields $+0.76$~pp on SciERC (5.8\% gap recovery) but $-0.64$~pp on CoNLL and $-3.21$~pp on Few-NERD. On degenerate subsets, merge is uniformly negative across all three datasets; entity-level aggregation cannot bypass the diversity bottleneck.
Hidden state probes (\S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}) confirm richer information exists ($+37$\% correlation) yet the gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ LP's $+4.8$\%), reinforcing the capability-diversity tension.
